**Michael Morhaime** (born November 3, 1967) is an American [video game developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer") and entrepreneur. He is the chief executive officer (CEO) and founder of [Dreamhaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreamhaven "Dreamhaven"), located in [Irvine, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irvine,_California "Irvine, California"). Morhaime is best known as the co-founder and the former [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_(corporate_title) "President (corporate title)") of [Blizzard Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blizzard_Entertainment "Blizzard Entertainment"), a subsidiary of [Activision Blizzard, Inc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision_Blizzard "Activision Blizzard")., that was founded in 1991 as Silicon & Synapse. He served on the Vivendi Games executive committee from January 1999, when Blizzard Entertainment, Inc. became a subsidiary of Vivendi Games, until July 2008.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Morhaime&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Morhaime was born into a [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") family and graduated from Granada Hills High School in 1985. He is also an alumnus of [Triangle Fraternity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle_Fraternity "Triangle Fraternity")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-3) and received his [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in Electrical Engineering in 1990 from the [University of California, Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles") (UCLA).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-UCLAHonorDinner2006_11_06-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-5)

In sixth grade, Morhaime, along with his brother and sister, purchased a video game console called the [Bally Professional Arcade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bally_Professional_Arcade "Bally Professional Arcade"), first released in 1978. Morhaime discovered that the console was programmable, and he taught himself how to write simple games on it, building off of example programming code he found in a gaming newsletter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-latimes_interview-6)

As an electrical engineering student at UCLA, Morhaime focused more on [hardware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_hardware "Computer hardware") than on [software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software "Software"). "I procrastinated a lot," he admitted.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-latimes_interview-6) Things changed after he got an internship at a [San Jose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose,_California "San Jose, California") microchip company. In his internship there, he learned about circuit design, and when he returned to school he was ahead of his computer architecture class. "I used to be the guy that sat in the back," he said, but after his stint in [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley"), he said, "I started sitting up front."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-latimes_interview-6)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Morhaime&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Blizzard Entertainment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Morhaime&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Blizzard Entertainment")]

While at UCLA, Morhaime bonded with [Allen Adham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_Adham "Allen Adham") after realizing they shared the computer password "Joe". Upon graduating, Adham persuaded Morhaime into forgoing his job offer at [Western Digital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Digital "Western Digital") to instead found Silicon & Synapse in February 1991, later renamed [Blizzard Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blizzard_Entertainment "Blizzard Entertainment").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-7) After hiring their friend and fellow UCLA alumnus, Frank Pearce, they rented a small office in [Irvine, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irvine,_California "Irvine, California"), hoping to benefit from nearby technology companies.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-latimes_interview-6)

In 1995, Blizzard released _[Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warcraft\_II:\_Tides\_of\_Darkness "Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness")_, its first number one selling game. "It's probably the game that put Blizzard on the map," Morhaime said. Besides its large number of sales, "it was the first game you could play over the Internet with a good experience," which was a novelty at the time, as well as being a defining selling point for its later titles.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-latimes_interview-6)

In planning for the release of _[World of Warcraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World\_of\_Warcraft "World of Warcraft")_ (_WoW_) in late 2004, Morhaime thought that the market for the much larger and more interactive new game, the first in their history to require players to pay a monthly subscription fee, would grow slowly. "We felt it was very likely the fee would be a deterrent for people, and that _WoW_ would not sell as quickly as some of our previous games," he said. All of Blizzard's production and marketing decisions were based on that assumption. To Blizzard's surprise, _WoW_ sold extremely quickly, leaving the underprepared Blizzard unable to keep merchants supplied with the game for a short time. "For the whole first year, we scrambled to keep up with demand," he said. "It probably took years off of our lives." _World of Warcraft_ had approximately 11 million subscribers as of 2010. In 2017, Morhaime earned $12.3 million as the CEO of Blizzard.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-8)

On October 3, 2018, Morhaime announced he was stepping down as the company president and CEO, instead becoming an advisor to the company. Morhaime was replaced by J. Allen Brack, the executive producer on _World of Warcraft_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-9) His advisory role concluded on April 7, 2019.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-10)

### Dreamhaven

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Morhaime&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Dreamhaven")]

In 2020, Morhaime founded [Dreamhaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreamhaven "Dreamhaven"), a video game company based in Irvine, California, with two internal studios: Secret Door and Moonshot Games.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-13)

In 2025, Dreamhaven published its first internally developed titles: **Sunderfolk**, a cooperative tactical RPG by Secret Door released on April 23 across PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and Nintendo Switch,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-14) and **Wildgate**, a crew‑based space‑shooter by Moonshot Games, which launched on July 22 on Steam, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-15)

## Controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Morhaime&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Controversy")]

Following Morhaime's departure from Blizzard, in July 2021, the [California Civil Rights Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Civil_Rights_Department "California Civil Rights Department") (CRD) (formerly known as the Department of Fair Employment and Housing) filed a lawsuit against Activision Blizzard for sexual harassment and gender-based discrimination in relation to unequal pay and retaliation against female employees in the workplace.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-16)

Amidst the news of the lawsuit, former Blizzard employees spoke out about their experiences and the harassment they witnessed within the company. A former manager at the then-competitive gaming brand FXOpen Esports, posted to social media about her experience at a Blizzard holiday party in which a senior creative director kissed her in front of a group of Blizzard employees, including Morhaime who was president and CEO at the time.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-18) While he was not named in the lawsuit, and some employees were uncertain whether he was aware of the allegations, multiple employees confirmed that Morhaime was present at some of the company events where the alleged misconduct took place. Morhaime tweeted an apology saying he was “ashamed” regarding the lawsuit several days after the news broke.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-20)

## Honors and awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Morhaime&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Honors and awards")]

In 2008, Morhaime was inducted into the [Academy of Interactive Arts and Sciences' Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Interactive_Arts_and_Sciences'_Hall_of_Fame "Academy of Interactive Arts and Sciences' Hall of Fame").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-21) On the same year, Morhaime was honored at the 59th Annual [Technology & Engineering Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_&_Engineering_Emmy_Award "Technology & Engineering Emmy Award") for Blizzard's creation of _[World of Warcraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World\_of\_Warcraft "World of Warcraft")_. Along with [Don Daglow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Daglow "Don Daglow") of [Stormfront Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stormfront_Studios "Stormfront Studios") and [John Carmack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Carmack "John D. Carmack") of [id Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Id_Software "Id Software"), Morhaime is one of only three designers or producers to accept awards at the Technology & Engineering Emmy Awards and at the [Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Interactive_Arts_&_Sciences "Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences")[Interactive Achievement Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interactive_Achievement_Awards "Interactive Achievement Awards").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-22)

Morhaime received the national [Ernst & Young Entrepreneur of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_&_Young_Entrepreneur_of_the_Year_Award "Ernst & Young Entrepreneur of the Year Award") in the Technology category in 2012.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-23) In 2019, Morhaime was appointed the 2019 Honor Award at the Gamelab Barcelona, in Spain for his success in the gaming industry.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-24)

## Multimedia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Morhaime&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Multimedia")]

In 2012, Morhaime made a cameo appearance on _[The Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guild\_(web\_series) "The Guild (web series)")_, a web series about the lives of a gamers' online experiences with an MMORPG that draws references to _World of Warcraft_. He is known for his work with the gaming community, but also worked on the 2016 film _[Warcraft: The Beginning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warcraft:\_The\_Beginning "Warcraft: The Beginning")_.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Morhaime&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Michael_Morhaime_and_Dave_Berggren_playing_with_L80ETC_at_BlizzCon_2009.jpg/250px-Michael_Morhaime_and_Dave_Berggren_playing_with_L80ETC_at_BlizzCon_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Michael_Morhaime_and_Dave_Berggren_playing_with_L80ETC_at_BlizzCon_2009.jpg)

Morhaime (left) playing with ETC at BlizzCon 2009

In 2010, Morhaime married his long-time girlfriend Amy Chen.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-wapo-1)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-25) In 2017, Morhaime bought a mansion in a gated [Rancho Mirage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rancho_Mirage,_California "Rancho Mirage, California") community in [Riverside County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverside_County,_California "Riverside County, California"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") for $2.25 million.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-26) He is a member of Elite Tauren Chieftain, a [metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") band formed of and by Blizzard employees, where he plays [bass guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morhaime#cite_note-27)

**William Murray** "**Trip**" **Hawkins III** (born December 28, 1953) is an American entrepreneur and founder of [Electronic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Arts "Electronic Arts"), [The 3DO Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_3DO_Company "The 3DO Company"), and [Digital Chocolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Chocolate "Digital Chocolate").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trip_Hawkins&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Trip_Hawkins_-_Summer_1987_Farther_magazine.jpg/250px-Trip_Hawkins_-_Summer_1987_Farther_magazine.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trip_Hawkins_-_Summer_1987_Farther_magazine.jpg)

Hawkins in 1987

A fan of the [Strat-O-Matic Football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strat-O-Matic_Football "Strat-O-Matic Football") pen and paper games, Hawkins started his first business as a teenager trying to create a knockoff version. He borrowed $5,000 from his father to start up the venture and advertised his game in NFL Game Programs, but the business failed. Eventually, he received his first computer and became interested in creating a digital football game, because it would allow players to avoid the challenging math of the game, which was all handled internally.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-OTLESPN-3)

He designed his own undergraduate major[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] at [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") in [Strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategy "Strategy") and Applied [Game Theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_theory "Game theory").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-smartcomputing-4)

Around this time, in 1975, Hawkins estimated that it would take home computer saturation seven years to make a viable career out of game design.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-OTLESPN-3)

In April 1977, Hawkins attended the first [West Coast Computer Faire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_Computer_Faire "West Coast Computer Faire"), where he saw the debut of the Apple II. The experience influenced his decision to join Apple Computer in 1978.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-5)

## Electronic Arts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trip_Hawkins&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Electronic Arts")]

He was the director of strategy and marketing at [Apple Computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") in 1982 when he left to found Electronic Arts (EA), a [video game publisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_publisher "Video game publisher"). EA was successful for many years under his leadership. He has been credited with spearheading the games industry's evolution from simple one-person creations to complex team projects during this time.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-6) One of his first big wins was to sign [John Madden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Madden "John Madden") on as a spokesperson and a consultant to his company's football game which would eventually lead to the popular _[Madden NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madden\_NFL "Madden NFL")_ series of video games.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-OTLESPN-3)

At this point, Electronic Arts was a computer software company which did not want to deal with Nintendo's strict licensing policies. He saw his opportunity when [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") released the [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Genesis "Sega Genesis"). Not wanting to pay licensing fees, he hired a team to [reverse engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_engineer "Reverse engineer") the system for his company to make unlicensed games on it. Hawkins eventually revealed his intentions to Sega, while offering a partnership to combat Nintendo telling them, "You can sue, but we did the tech fair and square and have great lawyers. So make us an official licensee. And give us a reduced rate." Sega, anticipating that Hawkins would sell his research to other third-party companies, agreed and made them a partner.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-OTLESPN-3)

## 3DO

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trip_Hawkins&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 3DO")]

Though he remained [chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chair_(official) "Chair (official)") of the board until resigning in 1994, he transitioned from EA in 1991 to form [3DO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_3DO_Company "The 3DO Company"), a [video game console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_console "Video game console") company. 3DO was formed in partnership with several other companies including EA. With its custom graphics hardware, the [3DO console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3DO "3DO") was the most powerful video game console at the time of its introduction in 1993. It launched at an expensive US$599(equivalent to about $1,400 in 2025),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-gamersatwork-7) compared to other major systems under $200. Sales were poor due to its price and weak games that relied excessively on [full-motion video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full-motion_video "Full-motion video") sequences at the expense of gameplay. Hopes for the system were further damaged in 1994 with the arrival of the [PlayStation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console) "PlayStation (console)") and [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Saturn "Sega Saturn"), both of which were less expensive than the 3DO[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-8) but had more modern hardware and stronger first party support. While acknowledging the 3DO's failure in the marketplace, _[Next Generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next\_Generation\_(magazine) "Next Generation (magazine)")_ listed Hawkins in their "75 Most Important People in the Games Industry of 1995", calling him "one of the game market's visionaries".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-9)

In 1996, 3DO stopped developing the system and transitioned into a [video game developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer"), making games for the PlayStation, [PC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible"), and other consoles.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-10) While remaining chairman and CEO of the company, Hawkins took on the additional role of creative director.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-11) Hawkins focused on branding and 6-to-9-month production timetables for games. As a result, quality and sales suffered. Hawkins had used cash reserves to bail out the failing company before, but declined to do so a final time. Due to poor sales of its titles, it went [bankrupt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankrupt "Bankrupt") in May 2003. The defunct company sold most of its [intellectual property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property "Intellectual property"), including the _[Might and Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Might\_and\_Magic "Might and Magic")_ franchise, to publisher [Ubisoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft "Ubisoft"), while Trip Hawkins retained ownership of the 3DO console hardware and software.

## Later career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trip_Hawkins&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Later career")]

In late 2003, Hawkins launched a new video game development company called [Digital Chocolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Chocolate "Digital Chocolate"). The company focused on developing games for [handheld devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_digital_assistant "Personal digital assistant"). They received high success with the mobile puzzle game _[Tower Bloxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower\_Bloxx "Tower Bloxx")_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-12) He stepped down from the [CEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CEO "CEO") position at Digital Chocolate in May 2012.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-13)

In 2012, Hawkins joined the board of directors of Israeli technology company Extreme Reality, which is working on developing motion control software that can read a person's movement in 3D, but which only requires a 2D camera.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-14)

On March 20, 2013, [Nativex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativex "Nativex"), a mobile ad technology platform for games, announced Trip Hawkins as a senior advisor to their board of directors.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-16) Hawkins also joined the advisory board at [Skillz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skillz_(company) "Skillz (company)"), a mobile eSports platform, as a strategic advisor in December 2014.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-17)

His newest startup, If You Can Company, aims to foster social and emotional development in children, teaching compassion and anti-bullying lessons. Their first game, "IF...", uses a [free-to-play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-to-play "Free-to-play") model and is meant for teachers and students in an educational environment.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-18)

Hawkins lives in [Santa Barbara, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Barbara,_California "Santa Barbara, California"), where he served from 2016 to 2019 as a professor of entrepreneurship and leadership at the [University of California, Santa Barbara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Santa_Barbara "University of California, Santa Barbara").

## Honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trip_Hawkins&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Honors")]

In 2005, Hawkins became the eighth person to be inducted into the [Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Interactive_Arts_&_Sciences "Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences") Hall of Fame.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-19)

**William Murray** "**Trip**" **Hawkins III** (born December 28, 1953) is an American entrepreneur and founder of [Electronic Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Arts "Electronic Arts"), [The 3DO Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_3DO_Company "The 3DO Company"), and [Digital Chocolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Chocolate "Digital Chocolate").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trip_Hawkins&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Trip_Hawkins_-_Summer_1987_Farther_magazine.jpg/250px-Trip_Hawkins_-_Summer_1987_Farther_magazine.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trip_Hawkins_-_Summer_1987_Farther_magazine.jpg)

Hawkins in 1987

A fan of the [Strat-O-Matic Football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strat-O-Matic_Football "Strat-O-Matic Football") pen and paper games, Hawkins started his first business as a teenager trying to create a knockoff version. He borrowed $5,000 from his father to start up the venture and advertised his game in NFL Game Programs, but the business failed. Eventually, he received his first computer and became interested in creating a digital football game, because it would allow players to avoid the challenging math of the game, which was all handled internally.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-OTLESPN-3)

He designed his own undergraduate major[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] at [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") in [Strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategy "Strategy") and Applied [Game Theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_theory "Game theory").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-smartcomputing-4)

Around this time, in 1975, Hawkins estimated that it would take home computer saturation seven years to make a viable career out of game design.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-OTLESPN-3)

In April 1977, Hawkins attended the first [West Coast Computer Faire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_Computer_Faire "West Coast Computer Faire"), where he saw the debut of the Apple II. The experience influenced his decision to join Apple Computer in 1978.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-5)

## Electronic Arts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trip_Hawkins&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Electronic Arts")]

He was the director of strategy and marketing at [Apple Computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") in 1982 when he left to found Electronic Arts (EA), a [video game publisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_publisher "Video game publisher"). EA was successful for many years under his leadership. He has been credited with spearheading the games industry's evolution from simple one-person creations to complex team projects during this time.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-6) One of his first big wins was to sign [John Madden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Madden "John Madden") on as a spokesperson and a consultant to his company's football game which would eventually lead to the popular _[Madden NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madden\_NFL "Madden NFL")_ series of video games.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-OTLESPN-3)

At this point, Electronic Arts was a computer software company which did not want to deal with Nintendo's strict licensing policies. He saw his opportunity when [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") released the [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Genesis "Sega Genesis"). Not wanting to pay licensing fees, he hired a team to [reverse engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_engineer "Reverse engineer") the system for his company to make unlicensed games on it. Hawkins eventually revealed his intentions to Sega, while offering a partnership to combat Nintendo telling them, "You can sue, but we did the tech fair and square and have great lawyers. So make us an official licensee. And give us a reduced rate." Sega, anticipating that Hawkins would sell his research to other third-party companies, agreed and made them a partner.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-OTLESPN-3)

## 3DO

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trip_Hawkins&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 3DO")]

Though he remained [chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chair_(official) "Chair (official)") of the board until resigning in 1994, he transitioned from EA in 1991 to form [3DO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_3DO_Company "The 3DO Company"), a [video game console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_console "Video game console") company. 3DO was formed in partnership with several other companies including EA. With its custom graphics hardware, the [3DO console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3DO "3DO") was the most powerful video game console at the time of its introduction in 1993. It launched at an expensive US$599(equivalent to about $1,400 in 2025),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-gamersatwork-7) compared to other major systems under $200. Sales were poor due to its price and weak games that relied excessively on [full-motion video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full-motion_video "Full-motion video") sequences at the expense of gameplay. Hopes for the system were further damaged in 1994 with the arrival of the [PlayStation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console) "PlayStation (console)") and [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Saturn "Sega Saturn"), both of which were less expensive than the 3DO[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-8) but had more modern hardware and stronger first party support. While acknowledging the 3DO's failure in the marketplace, _[Next Generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next\_Generation\_(magazine) "Next Generation (magazine)")_ listed Hawkins in their "75 Most Important People in the Games Industry of 1995", calling him "one of the game market's visionaries".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-9)

In 1996, 3DO stopped developing the system and transitioned into a [video game developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer"), making games for the PlayStation, [PC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible"), and other consoles.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-10) While remaining chairman and CEO of the company, Hawkins took on the additional role of creative director.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-11) Hawkins focused on branding and 6-to-9-month production timetables for games. As a result, quality and sales suffered. Hawkins had used cash reserves to bail out the failing company before, but declined to do so a final time. Due to poor sales of its titles, it went [bankrupt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankrupt "Bankrupt") in May 2003. The defunct company sold most of its [intellectual property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property "Intellectual property"), including the _[Might and Magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Might\_and\_Magic "Might and Magic")_ franchise, to publisher [Ubisoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft "Ubisoft"), while Trip Hawkins retained ownership of the 3DO console hardware and software.

## Later career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trip_Hawkins&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Later career")]

In late 2003, Hawkins launched a new video game development company called [Digital Chocolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Chocolate "Digital Chocolate"). The company focused on developing games for [handheld devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_digital_assistant "Personal digital assistant"). They received high success with the mobile puzzle game _[Tower Bloxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower\_Bloxx "Tower Bloxx")_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-12) He stepped down from the [CEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CEO "CEO") position at Digital Chocolate in May 2012.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-13)

In 2012, Hawkins joined the board of directors of Israeli technology company Extreme Reality, which is working on developing motion control software that can read a person's movement in 3D, but which only requires a 2D camera.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-14)

On March 20, 2013, [Nativex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativex "Nativex"), a mobile ad technology platform for games, announced Trip Hawkins as a senior advisor to their board of directors.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-16) Hawkins also joined the advisory board at [Skillz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skillz_(company) "Skillz (company)"), a mobile eSports platform, as a strategic advisor in December 2014.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-17)

His newest startup, If You Can Company, aims to foster social and emotional development in children, teaching compassion and anti-bullying lessons. Their first game, "IF...", uses a [free-to-play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-to-play "Free-to-play") model and is meant for teachers and students in an educational environment.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-18)

Hawkins lives in [Santa Barbara, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Barbara,_California "Santa Barbara, California"), where he served from 2016 to 2019 as a professor of entrepreneurship and leadership at the [University of California, Santa Barbara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Santa_Barbara "University of California, Santa Barbara").

## Honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trip_Hawkins&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Honors")]

In 2005, Hawkins became the eighth person to be inducted into the [Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Interactive_Arts_&_Sciences "Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences") Hall of Fame.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trip_Hawkins#cite_note-19)
