**Riot Games, Inc.** is an American [video game developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer"), [publisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_publisher "Video game publisher"), and [esports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esports "Esports") tournament organizer based in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"). It was founded in September 2006 by Brandon Beck and Marc Merrill to develop _[League of Legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League\_of\_Legends "League of Legends")_ and went on to develop [several spin-off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_League_of_Legends_media "List of League of Legends media") games and the unrelated [first-person shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-person_shooter "First-person shooter") game _[Valorant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valorant "Valorant")_. In 2011, Riot Games was acquired by Chinese [conglomerate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conglomerate_(company) "Conglomerate (company)")[Tencent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tencent "Tencent"). Its publishing arm, [Riot Forge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riot_Forge "Riot Forge"), oversaw the production of _League of Legends_ spin-offs by other developers until its shutdown in January 2024. The company worked with [Fortiche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortiche "Fortiche") to release _[Arcane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcane\_(TV\_series) "Arcane (TV series)")_, a television series based on the _League of Legends_ universe.

Riot Games operates [_League of Legends_ esports leagues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_Legends_in_esports "League of Legends in esports") and the [_Valorant_ Champions Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valorant_Champions_Tour "Valorant Champions Tour"). The company, which had 21 offices worldwide as of 2026, sells corporate sponsorships, merchandise, and streaming rights for its leagues. Riot has faced allegations and lawsuits alleging a toxic [workplace culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organizational_culture "Organizational culture"), including [gender discrimination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexism "Sexism") and [sexual harassment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_harassment_in_the_workplace_in_the_United_States "Sexual harassment in the workplace in the United States"). The company was criticized for its use of [forced arbitration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitration_clause "Arbitration clause") in response to these allegations.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Brandon "Ryze" Beck and Marc "Tryndamere" Merrill, the founders of Riot Games, became friends while roommates at the [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California"), where the two studied business.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Kollar16-3) Beck and Merrill believed too many video game developers diverted their focus from game to game too often, distinguishing _[Defense of the Ancients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense\_of\_the\_Ancients "Defense of the Ancients")_ as an indication that games could be supported and monetized long-term.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Kollar16-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-4) They also drew inspiration from Asian [video game designers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_designer "Video game designer") who released their games for no up-front cost, and instead [charged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microtransactions "Microtransactions") for additional perks.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5)

Beck and Merrill sought funding from family and [angel investors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_investor "Angel investor"), raising [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")1.5 million to launch their company.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5) Riot Games was established in September 2006 in [Santa Monica, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica,_California "Santa Monica, California").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-7) The first person Riot Games recruited was Steve "Guinsoo" Feak, one of the early developers of _[DotA Allstars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DotA\_Allstars "DotA Allstars")_, a game considered to have been foundational to the [MOBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplayer_online_battle_arena "Multiplayer online battle arena") genre.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Kollar16-3) As they refined _[League of Legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League\_of\_Legends "League of Legends")_' initial creation, they pitched investors a video game company rooted in [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce"). Merrill said that they approached publishers who were baffled by the game's lack of a single-player mode and [free-to-play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-to-play "Free-to-play") business model.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-8) Riot Games received several rounds of funding totaling $8 million, including investments by the [Benchmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benchmark_(venture_capital_firm) "Benchmark (venture capital firm)") and [FirstMark Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FirstMark_Capital "FirstMark Capital")[venture capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital "Venture capital") firms, as well as Chinese holding company [Tencent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tencent "Tencent"). The latter would later become _League of Legends_' distributor in China, and then the parent company of Riot Games.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-10)

Following six months of beta tests, Riot Games released _League of Legends_ as a [free-to-play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-to-play "Free-to-play") game on October 27, 2009.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Kollar16-3)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-11) Their game designers and executives participated in online forums to make adjustments based on player feedback.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5) On May 10, 2010, Riot Games announced that they would take over distribution and operation of their game in Europe; to do so, Riot Games relocated their European headquarters in [Brighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton "Brighton") to new offices in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-12) In February 2011, Tencent invested $400 million for a 93 percent stake in Riot Games.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-13) Tencent bought the remaining 7 percent on December 16, 2015; the price was not disclosed.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-14)

In 2012, in response to toxicity and harassment in _League of Legends_, Riot Games launched a "player behavior team" of psychologists to combat harassment on its platform.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Hess14-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-16) Riot Games' tactics to address issues on _League of Legends_, which included an opt-in chat function between opposing players, informing banned players of the reasoning behind the ban, as well as creating a tribunal of players to weigh in on bans, resulted in a 30 percent drop in reported harassment behavior.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Hess14-15) The efficacy of their results has been questioned by players and the gaming press.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-17) By 2013, _League of Legends_ was the most-played multiplayer PC game in the world.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-19) By 2016, _[Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inc.\_(magazine) "Inc. (magazine)")_ reported the game had over 100 million monthly players.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5)

Riot Games relocated to a new building on a 20-acre (8-hectare) campus in western [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") in 2015.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-20) In March 2016, Riot Games acquired [Radiant Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiant_Entertainment "Radiant Entertainment"), another developer who was working on _[Rising Thunder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rising\_Thunder\_(video\_game) "Rising Thunder (video game)")_ and _[Stonehearth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehearth "Stonehearth")_ at the time.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-21)_Rising Thunder_ was effectively canceled following the acquisition, with the game's team allocated to a new project.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-22)

On October 13, 2017, Beck and Merrill announced that they were returning their focus to developing games, aiming to create new experiences for video game and esports players.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Crecente17-23) Beck and Merrill handed over the day-to-day operations and overall management of the _League of Legends_ team to three longtime employees: Dylan Jadeja, Scott Gelb, and Nicolo Laurent, who previously served as [chief financial officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_financial_officer "Chief financial officer") (CFO), [chief technology officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_technology_officer "Chief technology officer") (CTO) and [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_(corporate_title) "President (corporate title)"), respectively.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Crecente17-23) Subsequently, Gelb and Laurent assumed roles as [chief operating officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_operating_officer "Chief operating officer") (COO) and [chief executive officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer") (CEO), respectively, while Beck and Merrill became the Riot Games' chairmen.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-24)As of May 2018[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit), Riot Games employed 2,500 people,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-25) operating 24 offices around the world.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-26)

In October 2019, Riot Games announced several new games: a version of _League of Legends_ for mobile devices and consoles called _[League of Legends: Wild Rift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League\_of\_Legends:\_Wild\_Rift "League of Legends: Wild Rift")_, a standalone mobile version of the _[Teamfight Tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teamfight\_Tactics "Teamfight Tactics")_ mode from _League of Legends_, and the [digital collectible card game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_collectible_card_game "Digital collectible card game") titled _[Legends of Runeterra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legends\_of\_Runeterra "Legends of Runeterra"),_ with all three scheduled for a 2020 release.[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-28) The company also teased further games — _Project A_, a [tactical shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tactical_shooter "Tactical shooter"); _Project L_, a [fighting game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_game "Fighting game") with _League of Legends_ characters; and _Project F_, a multiplayer game set in [Runeterra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runeterra "Runeterra") – that were not detailed outside of genre descriptions and brief gameplay clips.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-:1-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-:2-30)_Project A_ was later revealed to be _[Valorant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valorant "Valorant")_, which entered closed beta on April 7, 2020[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Webster_2020-31) and was officially released on June 2, 2020.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-espn-32)

In December 2019, Riot Games announced Riot Forge, a publishing label headed by Leanne Loombe. The label partnered with smaller game development studios for the creation of _League of Legends_ games, with some games of this type already being in development.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-33) Two titles from Riot Forge were announced at [The Game Awards 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Game_Awards_2019 "The Game Awards 2019"): _Ruined King: A League of Legends Story_ by [Airship Syndicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airship_Syndicate "Airship Syndicate"), and _Convergence: A League of Legends Story_ by Double Stallion Games.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-34) Another division, Riot Tabletop, was announced in January 2020, to produce [tabletop games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabletop_games "Tabletop games"); the first was _[Tellstones: King's Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tellstones:\_King's\_Gambit "Tellstones: King's Gambit")_, released in 2020.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-gibiz_tellstones-35)

Riot acquired Hypixel Studios in April 2020, which it had been investing in over the previous eighteen months to help it publish _[Hytale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hytale "Hytale")_, a [voxel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voxel "Voxel")-based sandbox game.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Riot_Games-36) Also in April, Riot announced plans to establish a [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore") office later that year. Riot Games Singapore is to support Riot's existing titles and will have a major focus on developing the company's newer titles.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-37) Jason Bunge was hired as Riot Games' [chief marketing officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_marketing_officer "Chief marketing officer") in October 2020.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-38) In October 2021, the company bought Kanga, a services firm involved in "fan hubs", merchandising, and content aggregation.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-39)

Riot Games collaborated with French animation studio [Fortiche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortiche "Fortiche") to release an animated series, _[Arcane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcane\_(TV\_series) "Arcane (TV series)")._ The series was released worldwide in November 2021 on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"), and by parent company Tencent in China, and received a favorable critical reception.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-41)

In March 2022, Riot Games announced that it had invested in Fortiche and, as a result, its [chief content officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_content_officer "Chief content officer") Brian Wright and director of [corporate development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_development "Corporate development") Brendan Mulligan were joining Fortiche's [board of directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-42) That same month, Riot also hired executives from Netflix, [Paramount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Global "Paramount Global"), and [HBO Max](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO_Max "HBO Max") to head development of film, TV, and music endeavors built around the company's intellectual property.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Variety22-44)

In October 2022, Riot acquired Wargaming Sydney—a subsidiary of Cyprus-based [Wargaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wargaming_(company) "Wargaming (company)") that had originally developed the MMO [middleware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleware "Middleware")[BigWorld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BigWorld "BigWorld")—for an undisclosed amount, and renamed it Riot Sydney. The acquisition excludes rights to the BigWorld technology itself, as well as its publishing arm.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-45)

In January 2023, Riot Games cut 46 employees in a round of layoffs.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-46) In the same month, it suffered a cyberattack that stole source code for League of Legends, Teamfight Tactics, and an anti-cheat platform. The hackers in question put the stolen data up for sale on the [dark web](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_web "Dark web") for US$700,000.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-48) In 2023, several games under the Riot Forge label were released, including [The Mageseeker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mageseeker "The Mageseeker") by Digital Sun, and [Song of Nunu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_of_Nunu "Song of Nunu") by [Tequila Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tequila_Works "Tequila Works"). In September 2023, Dylan Jadeja became company CEO.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-49)

Riot announced in January 2024 that it would be [laying off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023%E2%80%932024_video_game_industry_layoffs "2023–2024 video game industry layoffs") 530 employees, or about 11% of its workforce, as well as sunsetting the Riot Forge effort as well as its planned [Twitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitch_(service) "Twitch (service)") competitor, Riot Esports Network (REN). Jadeja stated the rationale for the layoffs: "A decision like this has a massive impact on people's lives and on the culture of Riot. We're not doing this to appease shareholders or to hit some quarterly earnings number – we've made this decision because it's a necessity. It's what we need to do in order to maintain a long-term focus for players."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-2024_layoffs-2)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-50) In May 2024, the company was sued in the [California federal court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_federal_court "California federal court") over its partnership with bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange [FTX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTX "FTX"). Lawyers for the plaintiff said the claims were brought as their losses from FTX could not be recovered due to the bankruptcy proceedings.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-51)

In June 2025, Riot Games announced the closure of Hypixel Studios, the development team behind the sandbox game Hytale, which the company acquired in 2020. After years of development, including a major engine rewrite and a delayed beta originally slated for 2021. Hypixel CEO Aaron Donaghey confirmed that the project could not be completed in a way that honored the original vision, leading to both the cancellation of Hytale and the phased wind‑down of Hypixel Studios.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-52)

## Esports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Esports")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/League_of_Legends_World_Championship_2017_Finals.jpg/250px-League_of_Legends_World_Championship_2017_Finals.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:League_of_Legends_World_Championship_2017_Finals.jpg)

The stage for the [2017 League of Legends World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_League_of_Legends_World_Championship "2017 League of Legends World Championship") finals between [SK Telecom T1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SK_Telecom_T1 "SK Telecom T1") and [Samsung Galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samsung_Galaxy_(esports) "Samsung Galaxy (esports)") in the [Beijing National Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_National_Stadium "Beijing National Stadium")

Riot Games operates esports leagues worldwide. This includes the [_League of Legends_ Championship Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_Legends_Championship_Series "League of Legends Championship Series"), comprising leagues in North America and Europe.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Spangler17-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Wolf18-54) In total, there are more than 100 teams in Riot Games' 12 regional leagues around the world.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-EngadgetConditt-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-DTZucosky-56) Teams compete over the course of a season separated into two seasonal splits.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Spangler18-57) Teams earn championship points to qualify for two major international competitions: the [Mid-Season Invitational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Season_Invitational "Mid-Season Invitational") and the [_League of Legends_ World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_Legends_World_Championship "League of Legends World Championship").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-59) Riot Games' World Championship is the annual professional tournament at the conclusion of each season.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Huddleston18-61)

During 2010 and 2011, the Riot Games team developed new content for _League of Legends_;[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Kollar16-3) it was during this time that the company realized that people also liked to watch the game being played.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Kollar16-3) As a result, Riot Games established its own _League of Legends_ esports leagues which produce weekly broadcasts and create a professional game schedule.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Kollar16-3) Following Riot Games' first world championship event in 2011, a small affair at a conference in Sweden, the company decided to turn their tournaments into professional sports-like events.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5) It invested in broadcasting equipment, hired sports programming producers, and trained [pro gamers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_gamers "Pro gamers") to be "TV-ready".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5) In 2012, Riot Games held its tournament at University of Southern California's [Galen Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galen_Center "Galen Center"), offering $1 million in prize money.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5) Riot Games has since held tournaments in Berlin, Seoul, [Madison Square Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Square_Garden "Madison Square Garden") in New York City, and the [Staples Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staples_Center "Staples Center") in Los Angeles.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5)

The company sells corporate sponsorships, merchandise, and streaming rights for its esports league.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5) In 2015, investors bought stakes in teams and began building their own squads.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5) Among the team owners in Riot Games' leagues are the owners of the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards"), [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Cavaliers "Cleveland Cavaliers"), [Houston Rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Rockets "Houston Rockets"), [Golden State Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_State_Warriors "Golden State Warriors"), [Philadelphia 76ers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_76ers "Philadelphia 76ers"), [Los Angeles Dodgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Dodgers "Los Angeles Dodgers"), [AOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AOL "AOL") co-founder Steve Case, and life coach [Tony Robbins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Robbins "Tony Robbins").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-63)_[Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inc.\_(magazine) "Inc. (magazine)")_ cited the growth of the leagues and high-profile ownership as part of its reasoning for making Riot Games its 2016 Company of the Year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5) Following debates over whether pro players and coaches should have a greater share of Riot Games' esports revenue and concerns raised about the company making in-game changes prior to matches, the company issued an [open letter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_letter "Open letter") in 2016 promising higher revenue shares and more collaboration with professional teams.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Blakely16-5) In 2017, Riot Games held the _League of Legends_ World Championship in China, with the finals taking place in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Huddleston18-61) The same year, the company announced it would franchise its ten-team North American _League of Legends_ Championship Series, which cost at least $10 million to enter.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-64)

In November 2020, Riot Games announced the first [_Valorant_ Champions Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valorant_Champions_Tour "Valorant Champions Tour"), the global competitive tournament for _Valorant_.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-65) In 2021, Riot began building out three new "remote broadcast centers" in Asia, North America (Seattle), and Europe (Dublin), as part of an effort to improve the scale of its esports productions using a centralized production model with regional hubs. The facilities would be capable of both on-site productions, and allowing regional productions to connect to the facilities' datacenters and use its infrastructure as part of remote productions. The three locations were chosen as their time zones are each eight hours apart, allowing them to "work a full shift and then shut down and throw control for the next productions to the next facility." The first RBC in Dublin, Ireland, opened in July 2022, in a building formerly housed by the nightclub The Wright Venue in [Swords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swords,_County_Dublin "Swords, County Dublin"); it has an IP-based infrastructure, six studios, and preserves the nightclub's [disco ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco_ball "Disco ball") (which had been promoted as the largest in Europe).[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-66)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-67) As part of its buildout of the LoL series, Riot partnered with the [FTX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTX_(company) "FTX (company)")[cryptocurrency exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency_exchange "Cryptocurrency exchange") in August 2021 for a seven-year deal. Following the [bankruptcy of FTX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_FTX "Bankruptcy of FTX") in November 2022, Riot began to seek legal methods to terminate the FTX contract.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-68)

## Criticism and controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Criticism and controversies")]

### Allegations over gender discrimination and sexual harassment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Allegations over gender discrimination and sexual harassment")]

Over the first half of 2018, _[Kotaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotaku "Kotaku")_ spoke to about 28 former and current employees at Riot Games. Several employees claimed that female employees at Riot were being discriminated against. For example, some noted that ideas from female employees were overlooked while the same ideas from male employees were readily accepted, and some female employees were groomed for more senior positions only to be passed up by a new male hire. These employees described Riot's working environment as a "bro culture". Other allegations included receiving images of male genitalia from colleagues and bosses, an email thread speculating on what it would be like to penetrate a female employee, and a list shared among senior staff members detailing which female employees they would sleep with.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-kotaku_gender-69)_Kotaku_ speculated that this came from Riot's history of generally catering to "core" gamers both in products and in hiring practices, causing the company to favor male employees over female employees.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-kotaku_gender-69)

Some Riot employees approached by _Kotaku_ asserted these accusations were not true or were already being addressed; for example, according to the head of the platform, Oksana Kubushyna, efforts to improve the hiring process to be more diverse and inclusive toward women started nine months before article's publication.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-kotaku_gender-69) Riot Games' corporate communications lead Joe Hixson acknowledged the problems and said they did not align with Riot's core values. Furthermore, he said that all Riot employees must be held accountable for the working environment.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-70)

In the week following _Kotaku_'s article, several more current and former developers came forward to speak on their own experiences at Riot, which included claims of sexual harassment and misgendering. In a statement to _[Gamasutra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamasutra "Gamasutra")_, Hixson indicated that the company is taking action based on the story and its response. He elaborated that, in regards to claims of misbehavior by higher-level executives at Riot, the seniority of the individuals would have no impact on disciplinary proceedings.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Gamasutra_Kotaku_followup-71) By the end of August 2018, Riot revealed it was implementing seven "first steps" to change the company's internal culture in light of the issues raised, including a "Culture and Diversity & Inclusion Initiative" priority.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-72) To help implement these, Riot hired [Frances X. Frei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_X._Frei "Frances X. Frei") as a senior adviser for diversity, leadership, and strategy.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-73)

As a response to the _Kotaku_ article, Riot offered a session at [PAX West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PAX_(event) "PAX (event)") in 2018 for prospective video game developers with a panel and one-on-one sessions to review [résumés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curriculum_vitae "Curriculum vitae"); the session only admitted women and [non-binary people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genderqueer "Genderqueer"). Members of Riot's game communities expressed outrage at the exclusion of men, while Riot employees defended the decision as such gender-exclusive support was necessary to correct the male-dominated nature of video game development. Some of the feedback towards Riot included harassment and threats. In response to a [shooting at a video game tournament in Jacksonville, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacksonville_Landing_shooting "Jacksonville Landing shooting"), in August 2018, Riot planned to increase security at its upcoming events.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-74) Two employees of Riot attempted to address the feedback from the PAX event; one was fired, and the other left the company. Riot stated that these departures were separate from its Diversity Initiative.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-75)

In December 2018, Riot's CEO Nicolo Laurent sent an email to all employees stating that following the company's internal investigation, its COO, Scott Gelb, was suspended for two months without pay for workplace misconduct and would take training classes before his return. Riot stated to _Kotaku_ that there were still other cases it was investigating, but they did not involve those as senior as Gelb, and thus it would not discuss these cases publicly.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-76) By January 2019, Riot updated the company values on its website, the first time since 2012, to reflect the apparent "bro culture" mentioned in the _Kotaku_ report,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-77) and by February 2019, had hired Angela Roseboro as the company's chief diversity officer to further help improve its culture by managing all activity related to diversity and inclusion as well as guiding the recruiting team in promoting inclusivity for new hires.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-78)

About three months after _Kotaku_'s story, one current and one former Riot employee filed a lawsuit against the company, asserting the company engaged in gender discrimination concerning their pay and position, and that the company had created a "sexually-hostile" workplace. The lawsuit seeks to qualify it as a class-action suit, and for damages to be based on unpaid wages, damages, and other factors to be determined at trial.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-79) Three other employees followed with their own lawsuits against Riot Games in the months that followed. Riot Games attempted to have two of the suits dismissed in April 2019, citing that the two female plaintiffs of these suits, when hired, had agreed to third-party [arbitration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitration "Arbitration") rather than taking court action.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-80) Internally, several employees of Riot threatened to walk out, an idea that had been around since the first _Kotaku_ article, as alongside the coercion to use arbitration, these employees felt Riot had yet to improve its transparency on the processes and had otherwise continued to retain Gelb despite his suspension.

A proposed settlement was reached in the class-action suit in August 2019, which would include at least US$10 million in damages to women that had been employed at Riot Games over the prior five years.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-81) Representatives of the class indicated that they thought it would lead to change, while Riot said that there were other issues not covered by the suit, and that it also intended to resolve the unacknowledged issues.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-82)

California's [Department of Fair Employment and Housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Department_of_Fair_Employment_and_Housing "California Department of Fair Employment and Housing") (DFEH) had been investigating claims of gender discrimination at Riot Games since October 2018. In June 2019, DFEH announced that Riot had denied providing them requested documents and were seeking action to compel these documents, though Riot responded by saying that it complied with all DFEH requests.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-83) Upon word of the settlement, the department filed a complaint with the court that stated they believed the settlement was far too low, estimating that the lawsuit potentially could have been worth as much as US$400 million. The state's [Division of Labor Standards Enforcement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Department_of_Industrial_Relations "California Department of Industrial Relations") also filed a complaint, believing the settlement would release Riot from labor liabilities that had been raised by the lawsuit. Both complaints urged the court to reject the proposed settlement.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-84) Riot dismissed the DFEH's larger value to the suit, and denied charges raised by the DFEH that it had colluded with the class's lawyer to reduce the amount it would pay through the settlement.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-85)

As a result of the state's findings that the terms of the settlement should have been valued higher, the class withdrew the proposed US$10 million settlement and dropped their original legal counsel, bringing on new lawyers who had been involved in prior lawsuits related to the [Me Too movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Me_Too_movement "Me Too movement") in February 2020.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-86) In response, Riot said it found the US$10 million figure "fair and adequate under the circumstances" after analysis, but were remaining committed to reaching a resolution.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-87) In August 2021, DFEH asserted that Riot was interfering in their ongoing investigations by falsely informing employees that they could not speak to DFEH directly; while the court ordered Riot to issue a memo to all employees that they legally could speak to DFEH, Riot had yet to comply with this order.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-88) By the end of 2021, Riot had agreed to a new settlement with the DFEH and employees of $100 million, with $80 million going to the impacted employees.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-89) The settlement was approved in July 2022.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-90) Riot will compensate 1,548 female employees between $2,500 and $40,000 each as part of the settlement.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-91)

Riot and Laurent were sued by Laurent's former assistant in January 2021 on sexual discrimination charges, which included inappropriate language and labor mistreatment.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-92) Riot opened an investigation by three members of its board of directors into Laurent's behavior in response to the lawsuit. They reported in March 2021 that "We concluded that there was no evidence that Laurent harassed, discriminated, or retaliated against the plaintiff. We have therefore concluded that at the current time … no action should be taken against Laurent."[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-93)

[Alienware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alienware "Alienware"), which had sponsored Riot's _League of Legends_ esports events, ended its partnership with Riot a year earlier than their contract term in March 2021 due to the ongoing litigation over the sexual harassment allegations.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-94)

#### Dispute over forced arbitration clauses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Dispute over forced arbitration clauses")]

Riot has also been criticized by its employees for requiring the use of forced arbitration in its employment contracts as a result of the gender discrimination lawsuit. Riot allowed employees to speak anonymously with the press, and indicated its intent to use town hall meetings and smaller group discussions with Roseboro and employees to determine future action.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-95) Riot also committed to removing mandatory arbitration in new employee contracts and potentially for existing ones after the current litigation had been settled.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-96) Additionally, Riot established a 90-day plan starting in May 2019 to continue to address internal issues related to diversity and inclusion.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-97) Despite this, over one hundred Riot employees staged their walkout on May 6, 2019, demanding that Riot end forced arbitration for all past and current employees as well.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-98) About two weeks following the walkout, Riot reverted its position, saying that it will not change forced arbitration in existing agreements while the current litigation against the company is ongoing.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-99)

### Others

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Others")]

#### Freedom of expression

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Freedom of expression")]

In the context of the [2019–2020 Hong Kong protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%932020_Hong_Kong_protests "2019–2020 Hong Kong protests"), Riot Games took action to discourage [political statements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_statement "Political statement") during its live events, claiming that overt statements on politics, religion, and other sensitive topics "cannot be fairly represented in the forum [their] broadcast provides", and has asserted that the company bears responsibility for ensuring "that statements or actions on [their] official platforms [...] do not escalate potentially sensitive situations."[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-100)

In 2019, players discovered that words that are politically sensitive in China, including _[Tiananmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiananmen "Tiananmen")_ and _[Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs")_, were censored in _League of Legends_. The censorship varied by server and language, with some restrictions being lifted after complaints were posted to [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit "Reddit").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-Liotta2019-101)

#### George Floyd

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: George Floyd")]

In June 2020, Ron Johnson, Riot Games' global head of consumer products, shared a [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") post that claimed [George Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Floyd "George Floyd") had been [murdered by police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_George_Floyd "Murder of George Floyd") "because of his criminal lifestyle". The company subsequently placed Johnson on leave to conduct an investigation, after which Johnson resigned from the company.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-102)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-103)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-105)

#### Sponsorship with Saudi Arabian city

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Sponsorship with Saudi Arabian city")]

Riot had announced a planned partnership with the developing city of [Neom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neom "Neom") in [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") in July 2020, with the city to sponsor the upcoming _League of Legends_ European Championship series. Shortly after the announcement, fans of the game, as well as Riot employees, criticized the company over social media and their streaming channels over the partnership, citing Saudi Arabia's record on [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Saudi_Arabia "Human rights in Saudi Arabia") and the violent attempts to evict the [Howeitat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howeitat "Howeitat") tribe from the area during the city's construction. Riot canceled the partnership within a few days in response, apologizing and saying that the partnership had been rushed.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-106)

#### Marketing using a character’s mental health struggles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Marketing using a character’s mental health struggles")]

Riot was criticized for marketing a new _League of Legends_ character, Seraphine,[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-auto-107) by creating an in-character [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") account in which it alluded to her struggles with her mental health, including low [self-esteem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-esteem "Self-esteem"), [anxiety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anxiety "Anxiety"), and [impostor syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impostor_syndrome "Impostor syndrome").[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-108) Some wrote that the account was an attempt to trick players into feeling close to her in an attempt to advertise.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-auto-107) Creative director Patrick Morales said that, although he was "proud" of the members of the team who worked on the campaign, it had "an unintended impact outside of the narrative we wanted to tell".[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-auto-107)

#### Response to Russian invasion of Ukraine

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Response to Russian invasion of Ukraine")]

After [Russia launched an invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine") in February 2022, Riot Games did not withdraw from the Russian market after being asked to do so by Ukrainian politician [Mykhailo Fedorov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mykhailo_Fedorov "Mykhailo Fedorov").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-109) In March 2022, Riot donated the proceeds from [battle passes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_pass "Battle pass") sold in several of its games, as well as profit from some in-game items, to humanitarian relief organizations operating in Ukraine.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-EngadgetBonifacic-110) According to Riot, these donations totaled $5.4 million.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-NMEGrimshaw-111)

## Litigation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Litigation")]

In 2017, Riot Games filed a lawsuit against [Moonton Technology Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonton "Moonton"), the developer of the mobile game _[Mobile Legends: Bang Bang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile\_Legends:\_Bang\_Bang "Mobile Legends: Bang Bang")_, because of copyright infringement, citing similarities between _Mobile Legends_ and _League of Legends_. The case was initially dismissed in California on account of _[forum non conveniens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forum\_non\_conveniens "Forum non conveniens")_. Tencent, on behalf of Riot Games, then filed a new lawsuit in a Chinese court, which ruled in Tencent's favor in July 2018, awarding it $2.9 million in damages.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-112)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-113)

In October 2019, Riot Games filed a lawsuit against Riot Squad Esports LLC, a [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago")-based esports organization founded in March 2019, alleging that Riot Squad intentionally infringed on Riot Games' "Riot" trademark.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-114)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-115)

### Tabletop games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Tabletop games")]

In October 2016, Riot Games released _[Mechs vs. Minions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechs\_vs.\_Minions "Mechs vs. Minions")_, a cooperative [tabletop game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabletop_game "Tabletop game") based on _League of Legends_.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-130)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-131) Riot's first tabletop game under Riot Tabletop was _[Tellstones: King's Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tellstones:\_King's\_Gambit "Tellstones: King's Gambit")_, a bluffing game for two or four players, released in 2020.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-132)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Merrill#cite_note-133)

### Card game

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Riot_Games&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Card game")]

In August 2025, Riot Games released [Riftbound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riftbound "Riftbound"), a multiplayer [trading card game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_card_game "Trading card game") set within the world of Runeterra.
