### Student media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Student media")]

_The Mercury_ has been the official student newspaper of the University of Texas at Dallas since 1980. It publishes 5,000 copies every other Monday during the fall and spring semesters, and every third Monday during the summer. It is distributed free around campus and at the UTD newsroom in the Student Union. _The Mercury_ also publishes online at utdmercury.com. In April 2011, _The Mercury_ won 12 awards at the 101st annual Texas Intercollegiate Press Association IPA convention.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-166) In September 2024, _The Mercury_'s editorial board, management team, and staff went on strike to protest the removal of Gregorio Olivares Gutierrez as Editor-in-Chief of _The Mercury_ and to demand his reinstatement by UTD's Student Media Operating Board.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-167) The team formed a new student paper, _The Retrograde_, which has been recognized by Student Government as the official student newspaper of UTD.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-168)_The Mercury_ returned in November of 2025, alongside _The Retrograde_.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-169)[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-170)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-171)

In 2004, another student print named _A Modest Proposal_ (_AMP_) was formed. In contrast to _The Mercury_, which is almost all news articles, _AMP_ is a magazine and features mostly editorial content. _AMP_ is published once a month, eight times a year. Any student, faculty, or staff of UTD can contribute to the paper. Copies of _AMP_ are available for free at the first of each month around the campus, and can also be downloaded in PDF format from their website.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-172)_Radio UTD_ is the university's student-run, online-only, radio station.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-173)

In 2009, UTD TV, an internet-based campus TV station, was founded and launched by students. It webcasts a range of student-interest programs from campus news and amusing serial stories to student affairs coverage.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-174)

### Residential housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Residential housing")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Residence_Hall_%28University_of_Texas_at_Dallas%29.jpg/250px-Residence_Hall_%28University_of_Texas_at_Dallas%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Residence_Hall_(University_of_Texas_at_Dallas).jpg)

On-campus housing for the 2015–2016 academic year consisted of the University Commons five residential halls and 1,237 apartments.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-UTD_Housing-175) The apartment buildings 1–37, which make up 696 units and buildings 38–67, which make up 541 units, are owned by the university and privately managed by American Campus Communities under the name University Village. Buildings 1–37, previously known as the Waterview Park Apartments, were owned by the Utley Foundation and purchased by UTD on July 1, 2013.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-Water_view_Park_Apartments-176)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-177) Apartment floor plans vary from 1-bedroom to 4-bedroom units and amenities include swimming pools, volleyball courts, outdoor grills, and study centers.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-178) According to a _UTD Mercury_ article on September 18, 2011, both graduate and upperclassman housing continues to be in short supply due to the increase in enrollment.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-179)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/UT_Dallas_Apartments.JPG/250px-UT_Dallas_Apartments.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UT_Dallas_Apartments.JPG)

UTD Apartments

On August 12, 2009, a 148,000-square-foot (13,700 m 2) residence hall (Residence Hall South) opened, providing housing for 384 full-time freshmen residents and 16 peer advisers. The building includes a mix of three-bedroom, single-bath suites for freshmen and one-bedroom, one-bath units for peer advisers. On each wing and each floor are several communal study areas and the ground floor features a 1,800-square-foot (170 m 2) glass-enclosed rotunda with pool and ping-pong tables, large-screen televisions, couches and chairs.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-ResHall-180) A second, 150,000-square-foot (14,000 m 2) residence hall, (Residence Hall North), was officially completed June 27, 2011, and a third freshman residence hall (Residence Hall Northwest) adjacent to the two existing halls was completed in August 2012. A fourth residence hall (Residence Hall Southwest) opened in time for the fall 2013 semester.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-University_Unveils_Plans_for_3rd_Residence_Hall-181)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-The_University_of_Texas_at_Dallas-182) Construction for a fifth residential facility (Residence Hall West) was started in July 2013 and completed in 2014. The 339,000-square-foot (31,500 m 2) 600-bed facility includes a dining hall with seating for 800 and a recreation center.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-183)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-184) Residence Hall West houses the Living Learning Communities program that groups students with similar interests and majors together.

Construction has begun on two new apartment-style housing complexes known as Phase VI and Phase VII.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-185) The two complexes will offer a total of 800 beds and are expected to open in time for the fall 2017 semester.[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

In 2015, co-developers [Balfour Beatty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balfour_Beatty "Balfour Beatty") Campus Solutions and Wynne/Jackson began construction of a private mixed-use development known as Northside on leased university land directly adjacent to the main campus.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-186) Opened in time for the fall 2016 semester, the development offers 600 beds through a mix of one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and townhomes. Northside also includes 20,000 square feet of space for retail and food vendors, bringing an integrated residential and retail complex to the edge of campus for the first time.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Traditions")]

The student body is collectively known as the Comets, while the college's mascot is Temoc. The "Whoosh" salute is a way for students to show campus unity.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:8-193)

Resting in front of the Texas Instruments Plaza is the sculpture _Jack_, created in 1971 by artist [Jim Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Love_(artist) "Jim Love (artist)") (1927–2005).[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-194) Margaret McDermott, wife of UTD founder Eugene McDermott (1899–1973), presented the sculpture to the university in 1976.

### Spirit Rocks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Spirit Rocks")]

The Spirit Rocks were a set of three "free speech" rocks on campus where students could paint anything following loose rules. The rocks were painted frequently with political, event-related, and school spirit messages.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-195)[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-196)

On October 16, 2023, student newspaper The Mercury reported on students spray painting [Palestinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Palestine "State of Palestine") and [Israeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") flags and messages on the Spirit Rocks in response to the [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war"). Students painted various messages in support of both countries, including "WE (Israel) ARE WINNING", "Free Palestine", "END OCCUPATION", "Terror ≠ 'Justice'", and "Zionism = Nazism". Dean of Students Amanda Smith said the support for both countries did not violate the rules of the Spirit Rocks.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:17-197) CBS Texas reported on the issue, calling the Spirit Rocks "a tense platform for politics with competing views about the violence in the Middle East".[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-198)

On November 20, the Spirit Rocks were removed by Student Affairs executives for platforming "extended political discourse" without consulting the committee responsible for university policies.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:16-199) This sparked backlash from the student body, prompting protests attended by hundreds of students.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-200) Free speech advocacy group [Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundation_for_Individual_Rights_and_Expression "Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression") condemned the university for the Spirit Rocks' removal.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-201) Students have since attempted to bring the Spirit Rocks back through Student Government[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-202), opinion articles[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-203), and artistic exhibitions.

## Athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Athletics")]

Main article: [UT Dallas Comets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UT_Dallas_Comets "UT Dallas Comets")

UT Dallas is transitioning to [NCAA Division II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_II "NCAA Division II") varsity athletics. It has competitive club teams and intramural sports teams. Athletic teams are known as the Comets, while the mascot is Temoc ("Temoc" is "comet" spelled backwards.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-204))

### Varsity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Varsity")]

The University of Texas at Dallas' Varsity athletics program started when UTD provisionally joined the [NCAA Division III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_III "NCAA Division III") and the [American Southwest Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Southwest_Conference "American Southwest Conference") (ASC) in 1998 and was granted full membership in the ASC in 2002.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-205)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:9-82) On July 20, 2023, the university announced it would move to [NCAA Division II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_II "NCAA Division II") and join the [Lone Star Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_Star_Conference "Lone Star Conference").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-auto-50) Varsity sports include baseball, basketball, cross country, esports, golf, soccer, softball, tennis, and volleyball.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-206)[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-207) In total, 300 student athletes and 14 intercollegiate teams are officially supported by the university.

Gene Fitch, the university's vice president of student affairs, stated that UTD plans to open "the premier collegiate gaming center in the country" by the spring of 2025.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-208)

### Intramural sports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Intramural sports")]

UT Dallas has several intramural sports teams.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-209) These teams compete only within UTD, as all teams are organized groups of current students. While available sports and teams can vary each year, teams offered in spring 2019 included badminton, basketball, Battleship, cricket, esports, flag football, sand volleyball, swim, soccer, table tennis, tennis, ultimate frisbee, wiffleball, rock climbing and Xtreme dodgeball.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-210)

The **University of Texas at Dallas** (**UTD** or **UT Dallas**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Richardson, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richardson,_Texas "Richardson, Texas"), United States. It is the northernmost institution of the [University of Texas System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_System "University of Texas System"). It was initially founded in 1961 as a private research arm of [Texas Instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments").

The university is [classified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-9) It is associated with four [Nobel Prizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") and has members of the [National Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_of_Sciences "National Academy of Sciences") and [National Academy of Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_of_Engineering "National Academy of Engineering") on its faculty with research projects including the areas of [Space Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outline_of_space_science "Outline of space science"), [Bioengineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_engineering "Biological engineering"), [Cybersecurity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_security "Computer security"), [Nanotechnology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanotechnology "Nanotechnology"), and [Behavioral and Brain Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behavioural_sciences "Behavioural sciences"). UT Dallas offers more than 140 academic programs[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-10) across its seven schools and hosts more than 50 research centers and institutes.

While the main campus is officially under the city jurisdiction of [Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richardson,_Texas "Richardson, Texas"), one-third of it is within the borders of [Dallas County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_County,_Texas "Dallas County, Texas"). UTD also operates several locations in [downtown Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Dallas "Downtown Dallas") – this includes the [Crow Museum of Asian Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crow_Museum_of_Asian_Art "Crow Museum of Asian Art") in the [Arts District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_District,_Dallas "Arts District, Dallas") as well as multiple buildings in the Medical District next to [UT Southwestern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_Southwestern_Medical_Center "University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center"): the [Center for BrainHealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_BrainHealth "Center for BrainHealth"), the [Center for Vital Longevity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Center_for_Vital_Longevity "The Center for Vital Longevity"), and the Callier Center for Communication Disorders.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Establishment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Establishment")]

Before the founding of the University of Texas at Dallas, [Eugene McDermott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_McDermott "Eugene McDermott"), [Cecil Howard Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Howard_Green "Cecil Howard Green") and [J. Erik Jonsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Erik_Jonsson "J. Erik Jonsson") had purchased [Geophysical Service Incorporated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geophysical_Service_Incorporated "Geophysical Service Incorporated") (GSI) on December 6, 1941 – the day before the [attack on Pearl Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor "Attack on Pearl Harbor"). With the rapid increase in defense contracts due to declaration of war with Germany, the General Instrument Division of GSI grew substantially and was later reorganized under the name [Texas Instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"), Inc. (TI) in 1951.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-11)

The increase in defense contracts also created a shortage in the [Dallas–Fort Worth area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas%E2%80%93Fort_Worth_metroplex "Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex") of the qualified personnel required by TI. At the time, the region's universities did not provide enough graduates with advanced training in engineering and physical sciences. Texas Instruments was forced to recruit talent from other states during its expansion, and the founders observed in 1959 that "To grow industrially, the region must grow academically; it must provide the intellectual atmosphere, which will allow it to compete in the new industries dependent on highly trained and creative minds."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-12)

To compensate for a shortage, McDermott, Green, and Jonsson established the Graduate Research Center of the Southwest on February 14, 1961. While the institute initially was housed in the Fondren Science Library at [Southern Methodist University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Methodist_University "Southern Methodist University"), a nearby empty [cotton field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottonfield "Cottonfield") was later acquired by Jonsson, McDermott, and Green in [Richardson, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richardson,_Texas "Richardson, Texas") in 1962. The first facility, the Laboratory of Earth and Planetary Science (later named the Founders Building), opened in 1964. The Graduate Research Center of the Southwest was renamed the Southwest Center for Advanced Studies (SCAS) in 1967.

On June 13, 1969, Texas governor [Preston Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Smith_(governor) "Preston Smith (governor)") signed House Bill 303, which added the institution to the [University of Texas System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_System "University of Texas System") as the University of Texas at Dallas (effective September 1, 1969).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-Handbook-13) When Texas Instruments and UTD co-founders officially bequeathed the young university to the UT System, they boldly stated that they envisioned it would one day become the “[MIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") of the South.”[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:12-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-15) At the time, the college only accepted [graduate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graduate_school "Graduate school") students for [masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") and [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") programs – no [undergraduate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate_education "Undergraduate education")[bachelor's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") degree programs were offered. Francis S. Johnson served as the initial interim president before Bryce Jordan was selected in 1971.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-16)

### Expansion and growth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Expansion and growth")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Engineering_and_Computer_Science_Complex_%28University_of_Texas_at_Dallas%29.jpg/250px-Engineering_and_Computer_Science_Complex_%28University_of_Texas_at_Dallas%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Engineering_and_Computer_Science_Complex_(University_of_Texas_at_Dallas).jpg)

Engineering and Computer Science South Building

In July 1971, [Bryce Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryce_Jordan "Bryce Jordan") became the university's first president and served until 1981.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-17) At that time the campus consisted of only one facility (the Founders Building) and only admitted graduate students. During Jordan's 10-year tenure the university received 275 acres (111 ha) of land in 1972 from the [Hoblitzelle Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoblitzelle_Foundation "Hoblitzelle Foundation"). This allowed the campus to expand with the addition of a number of new facilities, including most notably the Cecil H. Green Hall, the Eugene McDermott Library, and a campus bookstore.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-19) The school received accreditation from the [Southern Association of Colleges and Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Association_of_Colleges_and_Schools "Southern Association of Colleges and Schools") in 1972, and the first diplomas were awarded in 1973.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-20)

The first bachelor's degrees were awarded in spring 1976. The Callier Center for Communication Disorders became part of the UTD in 1975 and the School of Management opened in 1975.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-21) Enrollment increased from 700 in 1974, to 3,333 in 1975, and later to more than 5,300 students in 1977.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-Handbook-13)

UT Dallas's first [Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") laureate, the late [Polykarp Kusch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polykarp_Kusch "Polykarp Kusch"), was a member of the physics faculty from 1972 to 1982.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-22)

The first art installation, the _Love Jack_ by [Jim Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Love_(artist) "Jim Love (artist)"), was added to UTD's campus in 1976.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:12-14) The Visual Arts Building opened in 1978.

[Robert H. Rutford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_H._Rutford "Robert H. Rutford"), an Antarctic explorer recognized with the naming of the [Rutford Ice Stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutford_Ice_Stream "Rutford Ice Stream") and [Mount Rutford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rutford "Mount Rutford") in Antarctica, became the second president of UT Dallas in May 1982.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-Antarctic_Peak_named_for_Robert_Rutford-23) He served in this post until 1994. During his tenure as president, the university secured approval for a school of engineering, added freshmen and sophomores to its student body, and built the first on-campus housing.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-24)

The school became a four-year institution in fall 1990.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-26) The initial incoming freshman class was about 100 students. The state mandated that admission criteria for entering freshmen "to be no less stringent than the criteria of UT Austin".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-27)

[Franklyn Jenifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklyn_Jenifer "Franklyn Jenifer") became the third president of UT Dallas in 1994 and served until 2005. During that time, UT Dallas's enrollment increased over 61% – from less than 8,500 to nearly 14,000.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-28)

Parts of the university's ceremonial mace have been brought into space. A steel band in the headpiece and the metal foot of the staff fashioned from a scientific instrument designed by the UT Dallas Space Sciences Institute and were flown aboard the [Space Shuttle Endeavor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour") in September 1995.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-30)

The Galerstein Women's Center opened in 1996.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:12-14) It was renamed the Galerstein Gender Center and then dismantled in 2023 after the passing of SB17.

### Attempted DFW-area UT System mergers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Attempted DFW-area UT System mergers")]

In July 2001, the [77th Texas legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventy-seventh_Texas_Legislature "Seventy-seventh Texas Legislature") failed to pass two proposed bills which had very different plans for the future of the [Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas%E2%80%93Fort_Worth_metroplex "Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex")[UT System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_System "University of Texas System") intuitions.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:10-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-36)

The first plan, 77(R) HB 3568 proposed by [Kenn George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenn_George "Kenn George"),[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:11-37) would have consolidated the two universities and one medical school under the name "The University of Texas at Dallas".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:10-34) It would have established UT Dallas (UTD) in Richardson, Texas, as the main flagship campus, [UT Southwestern Medical Center at Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_Southwestern_Medical_Center "University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center") (UTSW) as its medical school, and would have designated [UT Arlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Arlington "University of Texas at Arlington") (UTA) as a UT Dallas [satellite campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_campus "Satellite campus") (a situation similar to [UT Rio Grande Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_Rio_Grande_Valley "University of Texas Rio Grande Valley")).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:10-34) The purpose of the bill was to consolidate all DFW UT System institutions into one, creating a single cohesive flagship-level university for the Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex. However, the bill was unpopular with supporters of UT Arlington (because they wanted to retain their identity as a separate institution from UT Dallas) and the House Bill ultimately failed to pass. Despite this, UT Dallas has continued a close relationship with UT Southwestern. UT Dallas' [Center for BrainHealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_BrainHealth "Center for BrainHealth") and Callier Center were built right next to UTSW's main campus in downtown Dallas. Additionally, UT Southwestern later established a Clinical Center in Richardson next to UTD's main campus.

The second plan, 77(R) HB 3607 proposed by [Domingo Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domingo_Garc%C3%ADa_(politician) "Domingo García (politician)"),[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:11-37) would have transferred UT Dallas, UT Southwestern, and UT Arlington to the [University of North Texas System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Texas_System "University of North Texas System") (to create something similar to the [University of Houston System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Houston_System "University of Houston System")).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:10-34) The [Denton, Texas campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Texas "University of North Texas") would have remained as the flagship university while the three Dallas–Fort Worth UT System institutions would have been designated as separate degree-granting sister UNT System colleges. Their names would have changed to the "University of North Texas at Dallas" located in Richardson, Texas (not to be confused with the present-day [UNTD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Texas_at_Dallas "University of North Texas at Dallas") campus established later in 2009), the "University of North Texas Southwestern Medical Center at Dallas" (UNTSW), and the "University of North Texas at Arlington" (UNTA).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:10-34) The law was left pending due to objections from both UT Arlington and UT Dallas, as both preferred to remain under the UT System.

In 2018, the university inherited the Barrett collection of Swiss art which will be housed in a new building as part of the Edith O'Donnell Institute of Art History.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-40) In January 2019, the family of Trammell and Margaret Crow donated the entire collection of the [Crow Museum of Asian Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crow_Museum_of_Asian_Art "Crow Museum of Asian Art") to UTD, along with $23 million in support funding to help build a structure on the university campus to show more of the artworks.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-41)

In fall 2019 UT Dallas marked its 50 years as a Texas public university (est. 1969), 44 years of undergraduate junior/senior enrollment (since 1975), 29 years of incoming freshmen enrollment (since 1990), and 58 years as a research center (founded in 1961).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-40_Years-42)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-43)

In April 2023, University of Texas at Dallas students protested the [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war") and [genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_genocide_accusation "Palestinian genocide accusation").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-45) They staged a sit-in and setup an encampment, [joining other campuses across the USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_pro-Palestinian_protests_on_university_campuses "2024 pro-Palestinian protests on university campuses"). The students demanded that the university [divest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boycott,_Divestment_and_Sanctions "Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions") from companies that contribute weapons to the war.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-46) The university administration called in riot police to forcibly remove the encampment and there were 17 arrests.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-48) UTD students were charged with trespassing on UTD land and threatened with disciplinary action.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-49)

On July 20, 2023, UT Dallas announced that it would leave the [American Southwest Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Southwest_Conference "American Southwest Conference") and transition to become an [NCAA Division II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_II "NCAA Division II") school in the [Lone Star Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_Star_Conference "Lone Star Conference").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-auto-50)

On August 26, 2024, UT Dallas President Richard C. Benson announced plans to step down from his position as the fifth president of the university. The [UT System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_System "University of Texas System") Board of Regents conducted a national search for his replacement over the course of the 2024–25 academic year, with Benson persisting in his role until a successor began their term, after which he would remain at the university in a faculty capacity.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-51) On May 7, 2025, the Board of Regents announced that Prabhas Moghe, former executive vice president for academic affairs at [Rutgers University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers_University "Rutgers University"), had been voted as the sole finalist for the sixth UT Dallas presidency. Moghe's experience with raising research funding at Rutgers was cited as a primary reason for his selection.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-52)

In September 2024, the student newspaper _The Mercury_ website was shut down by the administration and the editor removed,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-53) allegedly in retaliation for criticism of UTD actions against the pro-Palestinian protesters earlier in the year.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-54)

All freshmen admitted to the university are automatically considered for an Academic Excellence Scholarship (AES) Award. For the fall 2017 incoming freshmen class, the awards range from $3,000 per year for tuition and mandatory fees up to complete coverage of UT Dallas tuition and mandatory fees plus $3,000 per semester cash stipend to defray the costs of books, supplies and other expenses.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-84)

The McDermott Scholars Program, established at UT Dallas in 2000, provides full scholarships and unique cultural and civic opportunities to academically talented high school students.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-Eugene_McDermott_Scholars_Program-85)

In 2006, UT Dallas became one of 13 universities in Texas affiliated with the Terry Foundation Scholarship. The Terry Scholars Program is a cohort experience that offers academic, cultural, service, mentoring, and other unique opportunities to traditional and transfer students awarded the prestigious scholarship.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-TerryScholars-87)

Hanson Center for Space Studies (CSS), affiliated with the Department of Physics, conducts research in space [plasma physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_physics "Plasma physics"). It has its roots in the Earth and Planetary Sciences Laboratory of the university's predecessor. The center conducts a NASA-sponsored mission, [Coupled Ion-Neutral Dynamics Investigation (CINDI)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CINDI "CINDI"), which was launched in April 2008 in cooperation with the United States Air Force.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-93) CINDI, which is part of the payload for the [Communication and Navigation Outage Forecast System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C/NOFS "C/NOFS") program, seeks to uncover information about the [equatorial plasma bubbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_plasma_bubble "Equatorial plasma bubble") that interrupt radio signals.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-94)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-95) Under the leadership of [John H. Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_H._Hoffman "John H. Hoffman"), the center designed the [mass spectrometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_spectrometer "Mass spectrometer") for the [Phoenix Mars Lander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Mars_Lander "Phoenix Mars Lander") as part of the [Thermal and Evolved Gas Analyzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_and_Evolved_Gas_Analyzer "Thermal and Evolved Gas Analyzer") (TEGA) experiment in cooperation with the [University of Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Arizona "University of Arizona").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-marsexp-96)

UT Dallas conducts cybersecurity research in a number of areas including cross-domain information sharing, data security and privacy, data mining for malware detection, geospatial information security, secure social networks, and secure cloud computing.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-97) The university is designated a National Center of Academic Excellence in Information Assurance Research for the academic years 2008–2013 by the [National Security Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Agency "National Security Agency") and [Department of Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Homeland_Security "Department of Homeland Security").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-98)

The [Alan G. MacDiarmid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_G._MacDiarmid "Alan G. MacDiarmid") NanoTech Institute was established in 2001 when Ray Baughman, a pioneering nanotechnologist, became the Robert A. Welch Distinguished Chair in Chemistry and director of the university's NanoTech Institute. In 2007, it was renamed in memory of the late [Alan G. MacDiarmid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_MacDiarmid "Alan MacDiarmid"), who shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in chemistry with [Alan Heeger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Heeger "Alan Heeger") and [Hideki Shirakawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Shirakawa "Hideki Shirakawa") for the discovery and development of conductive polymers. The NanoTech Institute has produced more than 200 refereed journal articles, 13 of which have been published in _[Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_(journal) "Science (journal)")_ or _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_, and given over 300 lectures in the United States and abroad.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-Alan_G._MacDiarmid_NanoTech_Institute_Publications-99) Ray Baughman was ranked number 30 on the March 2, 2011, Thomson Reuters list of the top 100 materials scientists.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-100)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-101)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Natural_Science_Engineering_and_Research_Lab_building_%28University_of_Texas_at_Dallas%29.jpg/250px-Natural_Science_Engineering_and_Research_Lab_building_%28University_of_Texas_at_Dallas%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Natural_Science_Engineering_and_Research_Lab_building_(University_of_Texas_at_Dallas).jpg)

Natural Science and Engineering Research Laboratory

The Natural Science and Engineering Research Laboratory (NSERL), a four-story, 192,000-square-foot (17,800 m 2) research facility, was completed in December 2006 after two years of construction. Including [ISO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_14644-1 "ISO 14644-1")[7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_1000_(standard) "Class 1000 (standard)")[cleanroom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleanroom "Cleanroom") facilities, the $85 million building provides open floor plans that allows chemists, biologists, nanotechnologists, materials scientists and other specialists to conduct multidisciplinary research. The laboratory provides extensive wet lab, fabrication, instrumentation, and high performance computing facilities to foster biomedical engineering and nano-technology research. The [Nanoelectronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanoelectronics "Nanoelectronics") Materials Laboratory, on the fourth floor, includes a system that allows researchers to deposit thin film materials one atomic layer at a time. In May 2011 a $3 million JEOL ARM200F scanning transmission electron microscope with an atomic resolution of 0.78 [picometers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picometers "Picometers"), was added to the research laboratory, already home to two transmission electron microscopes.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-Texas_Icon_H._Ross_Perot_highlights_Dedication_of_UTD's_Natural_Science_&_Engineering_Research_Laboratory-102)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-103)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-104)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Outside_of_bh_wiki.jpg/250px-Outside_of_bh_wiki.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Outside_of_bh_wiki.jpg)

Center for BrainHealth

The [Center for BrainHealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_BrainHealth "Center for BrainHealth"), both its own facility and part of the School of Behavioral and Brain Sciences, is a research institute with clinical interventions focused on brain health. The center is located near the UT Dallas' Callier Center for Communication Disorders and adjacent to the north campus of [University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_Southwestern_Medical_Center "University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center") in the city of Dallas. Brain research is concentrated on brain conditions, diseases, and disorders including, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, autism, dementia, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and working memory.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-brainhealth.utdallas-105)

The Callier Center for Communication Disorders became part of the University of Texas at Dallas in 1975 as part of the School of Human Development (now the School of Behavioral and Brain Sciences). Research, at the center, includes the causes, prevention, assessment and treatment of communication disorders and the facilities include laboratories for research in child language development and disorders, autism spectrum disorders, speech production, hearing disorders, neurogenic speech and language, cochlear implants and aural habilitation.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-106)

Additional ongoing research initiatives at UT Dallas include researchers overseeing the long-running [British Election Study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Election_Study "British Election Study") (BES). Harold Clarke, the Ashbel Smith professor of political science in the School of Economic, Political and Policy Sciences, and Marianne Stewart, professor of political science are the co-principal investigators for the study, which began in 1964 and is one of the world's oldest continuous political research projects. The other two co-investigators are David Sanders and Paul Whiteley of the [University of Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Essex "University of Essex") in England.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-107)

### Main campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Main campus")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/UTD_Visitor_Center.jpg/250px-UTD_Visitor_Center.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UTD_Visitor_Center.jpg)

UTD Visitor Center

The main campus is located in [Richardson, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richardson,_Texas "Richardson, Texas"). Small portions of that campus extend into [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-108) The main campus is next to Dallas's [Telecom Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecom_Corridor "Telecom Corridor"), 18 miles (29 km) north of downtown Dallas, on the boundary of [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_County,_Texas "Dallas County, Texas") and [Collin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_County,_Texas "Collin County, Texas") counties. UT Dallas owns land in Richardson, Texas consisting of approximately 465 acres (1.88 km 2) for campus development and another 265 acres (1.07 km 2) adjacent to the campus.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-Facilities_Management-109)_The Princeton Review's Guide to 332 Green Colleges: 2014 Edition_ recognized UTD for their green campus efforts.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-110)

While the main campus' address is officially within the jurisdiction of Richardson and Collin County, approximately one-third of the campus today (one-half in 1969) is located within Dallas County. This section contains major areas in the south end of campus, including the Visitor Center, Bookstore, the Naveen Jindal School of Management, Athletics District and facilities, half of the Founders Building, parking lots, and some on-campus student housing (Canyon Creek and University Village buildings 1, 2, and 3).[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-111)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-112) When UT Dallas started growing in the 1960s, the university needed to coordinate with one of the cities for water, electricity, sewer, police, and fire services. Dallas agreed to let Richardson officially host the university because it did not have the ability or capacity to support UTD at the time (a situation similar to [SMU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Methodist_University "Southern Methodist University") and [University Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Park,_Texas "University Park, Texas")).[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-113) Today, UT Dallas and Richardson share a close relationship and have strongly supported each other's growth for the past 50 years.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-114)

### Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/UT_Dallas_Student_Service_Building.JPG/250px-UT_Dallas_Student_Service_Building.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UT_Dallas_Student_Service_Building.JPG)

Student Services building

The first campus development plan (1971) called for [brutalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutalist_architecture "Brutalist architecture")-style concrete architecture, a [monorail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monorail "Monorail"), and skywalks.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:12-14) While not everything was implemented, some of the original elements outlined do remain today. The overall modern look and feel of the campus was inspired by the founders' vision of a "college of the future" – intentionally straying far from the traditional "red-brick" styles of older universities.

Later architecture (early 21st century) exhibits late modern or [postmodern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodern_architecture "Postmodern architecture") features such as bronze glass, bronze aluminum frames, unadorned geometric shapes, unusual surfaces, and unorthodox layouts. This styling is seen in the Engineering and Computer Science West building, School of Management, Cecil and Ida Green Center, and Natural Science and Engineering Research Lab facility (called the Mermaid Building due to its colorful anodized shingles). To provide protection from inclement weather and extreme temperatures, many of the buildings on campus are connected by a series of elevated indoor walking paths also referred to as [skybridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyway "Skyway").[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-124)

The Student Services building, completed in 2010, is the first academic structure in Texas to be rated a [LEED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_in_Energy_and_Environmental_Design "Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design") Platinum facility by the [United States Green Building Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Green_Building_Council "U.S. Green Building Council").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-125)

### Landscape

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Landscape")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/UTD_mall.JPG/250px-UTD_mall.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UTD_mall.JPG)

The Plinth, located between the McDermott Library (left) and the Student Union (right)

A $30 million Campus Landscape Enhancement Project, largely funded by Margaret McDermott (wife of UTD founder Eugene McDermott), was started in October 2008 and completed in late 2010. The project encompassed all aspects of landscape architecture from campus identity to pedestrian strategies, future growth patterns, sustainability and establishing a campus core. The first enhancement included the reforestation of the main entry drive with more than 5,000 native trees. Each tree was hand-picked and individually arranged by the landscape architect after study of native stands in Texas.

The next major enhancement included the commitment to a [riparian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riparian_zone "Riparian zone") corridor, consisting of a densely planted natural creek bed along the central entry median to the campus [Allée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_(landscape) "Avenue (landscape)"). The main Mall (or 'Allée') includes 116 hand-picked columnar 'Claudia Wannamaker' Magnolias alongside five reflecting pools and four human-scale chess boards (to represent the achievements of the school's chess team). At the northern terminus of the Mall (between the McDermott Library and the Student Union) is a pavilion-sized plaza, referred to by many students as "The Plinth". The plaza includes a granite fountain complete with mist column, an overhead trellis covered in [wisteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisteria "Wisteria") vines, and a temperature-modifying shade structure design.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-126)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-127)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-128)

The most recent Phase of the Campus Landscape Enhancement Project was completed in time for the fall 2021 semester. This phase included converting a section of Rutford Ave from North Loop Road to Franklyn Jenifer Drive into a 24-foot wide pedestrian-only promenade. Six brick signs matching that of the main entrance was also installed at major intersections and campus entrances. A bridge was also installed over Cottonwood Creek between Callier Center Richardson and the Bioengineering and Sciences Building which was finished in September 2021.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-129) A total of 1,200 trees were planted and enhancements were made to the Rock Garden behind the Founder Building.

### Art museum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Art museum")]

In November 2018, the university announced the donation of the Barrett Collection of Swiss Art, the largest collection of Swiss art outside of Switzerland. Shortly after, in January 2019, the family of Trammell and Margaret Crow, local real estate mogul, donated the entire collection of the Crow Museum of Asian Art to The University of Texas at Dallas, along with $23 million in support funding to help build a structure on the university campus to show more of the artworks. This donation was a decade in the making by the Director of the Center for Asian Studies and Dean of the then School of Arts and Humanities, Dennis M. Kratz.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-130)

With the need to build an art museum to hold these vast collections, Richard Brettell, founding director of the Edith O'Donnell Institute of Art History and major orchestrator of the two acquisitions, was heavily involved in the design process,[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-131) which was designed by the Los Angeles-based architecture firm Morphosis, which is also designed the renowned Perot Museum of Nature and Science in Downtown Dallas[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-132)

Located south of the Naveen Jindal School of Management and close to the main entrance of the university, groundbreaking for the two story 68, 459 sq ft Edith and Peter O’Donnell Jr. Athenaeum began on May 11, 2022, and is expected to be completed by 2024. The project is expected to cost $58 million, with around 55% of the cost being funded through university gifts.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-133) Upon completion, the Athenaeum will be the largest major art museum north of I-635.

#### Chess

The internationally ranked UT Dallas chess team was launched in 1996 under the direction of two-time president of the U.S. Chess Federation, Timothy Redman.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-135) The university recruits worldwide for its chess team and 24 [Grandmasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_(chess) "Grandmaster (chess)") and [International Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Master_(chess) "International Master (chess)") have played for UT Dallas from 1996 to 2018. ### Greek life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Greek life")]

The University of Texas at Dallas opened the Office of Fraternity and Sorority Life in 1992 with [Kappa Sigma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kappa_Sigma "Kappa Sigma") and [Alpha Gamma Delta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Gamma_Delta "Alpha Gamma Delta") as the first fraternity and sorority on campus, respectively. Internal sources state that more than 1,000 students are involved in 26 Greek organizations as of fall 2019.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-165)

### Student media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Student media")]

_The Mercury_ has been the official student newspaper of the University of Texas at Dallas since 1980. It publishes 5,000 copies every other Monday during the fall and spring semesters, and every third Monday during the summer. It is distributed free around campus and at the UTD newsroom in the Student Union. _The Mercury_ also publishes online at utdmercury.com. In April 2011, _The Mercury_ won 12 awards at the 101st annual Texas Intercollegiate Press Association IPA convention.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-166) In September 2024, _The Mercury_'s editorial board, management team, and staff went on strike to protest the removal of Gregorio Olivares Gutierrez as Editor-in-Chief of _The Mercury_ and to demand his reinstatement by UTD's Student Media Operating Board.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-167) The team formed a new student paper, _The Retrograde_, which has been recognized by Student Government as the official student newspaper of UTD.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-168)_The Mercury_ returned in November of 2025, alongside _The Retrograde_.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-169)[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-170)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-171)

In 2004, another student print named _A Modest Proposal_ (_AMP_) was formed. In contrast to _The Mercury_, which is almost all news articles, _AMP_ is a magazine and features mostly editorial content. _AMP_ is published once a month, eight times a year. Any student, faculty, or staff of UTD can contribute to the paper. Copies of _AMP_ are available for free at the first of each month around the campus, and can also be downloaded in PDF format from their website.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-172)_Radio UTD_ is the university's student-run, online-only, radio station.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-173)

In 2009, UTD TV, an internet-based campus TV station, was founded and launched by students. It webcasts a range of student-interest programs from campus news and amusing serial stories to student affairs coverage.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-174)

### Residential housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Residential housing")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Residence_Hall_%28University_of_Texas_at_Dallas%29.jpg/250px-Residence_Hall_%28University_of_Texas_at_Dallas%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Residence_Hall_(University_of_Texas_at_Dallas).jpg)

UTD Residence Hall South

On-campus housing for the 2015–2016 academic year consisted of the University Commons five residential halls and 1,237 apartments.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-UTD_Housing-175) The apartment buildings 1–37, which make up 696 units and buildings 38–67, which make up 541 units, are owned by the university and privately managed by American Campus Communities under the name University Village. Buildings 1–37, previously known as the Waterview Park Apartments, were owned by the Utley Foundation and purchased by UTD on July 1, 2013.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-Water_view_Park_Apartments-176)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-177) Apartment floor plans vary from 1-bedroom to 4-bedroom units and amenities include swimming pools, volleyball courts, outdoor grills, and study centers.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-178) According to a _UTD Mercury_ article on September 18, 2011, both graduate and upperclassman housing continues to be in short supply due to the increase in enrollment.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-179)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/UT_Dallas_Apartments.JPG/250px-UT_Dallas_Apartments.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UT_Dallas_Apartments.JPG)

UTD Apartments

On August 12, 2009, a 148,000-square-foot (13,700 m 2) residence hall (Residence Hall South) opened, providing housing for 384 full-time freshmen residents and 16 peer advisers. The building includes a mix of three-bedroom, single-bath suites for freshmen and one-bedroom, one-bath units for peer advisers. On each wing and each floor are several communal study areas and the ground floor features a 1,800-square-foot (170 m 2) glass-enclosed rotunda with pool and ping-pong tables, large-screen televisions, couches and chairs.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-ResHall-180) A second, 150,000-square-foot (14,000 m 2) residence hall, (Residence Hall North), was officially completed June 27, 2011, and a third freshman residence hall (Residence Hall Northwest) adjacent to the two existing halls was completed in August 2012. A fourth residence hall (Residence Hall Southwest) opened in time for the fall 2013 semester.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-University_Unveils_Plans_for_3rd_Residence_Hall-181)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-The_University_of_Texas_at_Dallas-182) Construction for a fifth residential facility (Residence Hall West) was started in July 2013 and completed in 2014. The 339,000-square-foot (31,500 m 2) 600-bed facility includes a dining hall with seating for 800 and a recreation center.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-183)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-184) Residence Hall West houses the Living Learning Communities program that groups students with similar interests and majors together.

Construction has begun on two new apartment-style housing complexes known as Phase VI and Phase VII.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-185) The two complexes will offer a total of 800 beds and are expected to open in time for the fall 2017 semester.[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

In 2015, co-developers [Balfour Beatty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balfour_Beatty "Balfour Beatty") Campus Solutions and Wynne/Jackson began construction of a private mixed-use development known as Northside on leased university land directly adjacent to the main campus.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-186) Opened in time for the fall 2016 semester, the development offers 600 beds through a mix of one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and townhomes. Northside also includes 20,000 square feet of space for retail and food vendors, bringing an integrated residential and retail complex to the edge of campus for the first time.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Dining")]

Students have multiple dining options, including commercial restaurants primarily within the Student Union, a traditional dining hall near the residence halls, and convenience stores within buildings. Commercial restaurants include [Firehouse Subs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firehouse_Subs "Firehouse Subs"), [Chick-fil-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick-fil-A "Chick-fil-A"), [Smoothie King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoothie_King "Smoothie King"), [Halal Guys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Halal_Guys "The Halal Guys"), [Panda Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panda_Express "Panda Express"), [Starbucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starbucks "Starbucks"), and [Einstein Bros. Bagels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_Bros._Bagels "Einstein Bros. Bagels").[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-187)[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-188) The Student Union dining hall opened on August 12, 2009, in conjunction with the opening of the first residence hall and was later replaced by a new dining hall within the Residence Hall West complex.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-189)[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-190) The former Student Union dining hall was later replaced by an extended food court area featuring an expanded Chick-fil-A and a Panda Express, among other options. The Student Union building houses The Pub which features a sit-down restaurant atmosphere.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-191) Beginning in the fall 2016 semester, UT Dallas Dining began hosting local food trucks on campus. All first-year students living on campus are required to purchase a meal plan; meal plans are optional for all other students who live on campus.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-192)

## Traditions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Traditions")]

The student body is collectively known as the Comets, while the college's mascot is Temoc. The "Whoosh" salute is a way for students to show campus unity.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:8-193)

Resting in front of the Texas Instruments Plaza is the sculpture _Jack_, created in 1971 by artist [Jim Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Love_(artist) "Jim Love (artist)") (1927–2005).[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-194) Margaret McDermott, wife of UTD founder Eugene McDermott (1899–1973), presented the sculpture to the university in 1976.

### Spirit Rocks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Spirit Rocks")]

The Spirit Rocks were a set of three "free speech" rocks on campus where students could paint anything following loose rules. The rocks were painted frequently with political, event-related, and school spirit messages.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-195)[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-196)

On October 16, 2023, student newspaper The Mercury reported on students spray painting [Palestinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Palestine "State of Palestine") and [Israeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") flags and messages on the Spirit Rocks in response to the [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war"). Students painted various messages in support of both countries, including "WE (Israel) ARE WINNING", "Free Palestine", "END OCCUPATION", "Terror ≠ 'Justice'", and "Zionism = Nazism". Dean of Students Amanda Smith said the support for both countries did not violate the rules of the Spirit Rocks.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:17-197) CBS Texas reported on the issue, calling the Spirit Rocks "a tense platform for politics with competing views about the violence in the Middle East".[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-198)

On November 20, the Spirit Rocks were removed by Student Affairs executives for platforming "extended political discourse" without consulting the committee responsible for university policies.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:16-199) This sparked backlash from the student body, prompting protests attended by hundreds of students.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-200) Free speech advocacy group [Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundation_for_Individual_Rights_and_Expression "Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression") condemned the university for the Spirit Rocks' removal.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-201) Students have since attempted to bring the Spirit Rocks back through Student Government[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-202), opinion articles[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-203), and artistic exhibitions.

## Athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Athletics")]

Main article: [UT Dallas Comets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UT_Dallas_Comets "UT Dallas Comets")

UT Dallas is transitioning to [NCAA Division II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_II "NCAA Division II") varsity athletics. It has competitive club teams and intramural sports teams. Athletic teams are known as the Comets, while the mascot is Temoc ("Temoc" is "comet" spelled backwards.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-204))

### Varsity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Varsity")]

The University of Texas at Dallas' Varsity athletics program started when UTD provisionally joined the [NCAA Division III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_III "NCAA Division III") and the [American Southwest Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Southwest_Conference "American Southwest Conference") (ASC) in 1998 and was granted full membership in the ASC in 2002.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-205)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-:9-82) On July 20, 2023, the university announced it would move to [NCAA Division II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_II "NCAA Division II") and join the [Lone Star Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lone_Star_Conference "Lone Star Conference").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-auto-50) Varsity sports include baseball, basketball, cross country, esports, golf, soccer, softball, tennis, and volleyball.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-206)[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-207) In total, 300 student athletes and 14 intercollegiate teams are officially supported by the university.

Gene Fitch, the university's vice president of student affairs, stated that UTD plans to open "the premier collegiate gaming center in the country" by the spring of 2025.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-208)

### Intramural sports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Texas_at_Dallas&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Intramural sports")]

UT Dallas has several intramural sports teams.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-209) These teams compete only within UTD, as all teams are organized groups of current students. While available sports and teams can vary each year, teams offered in spring 2019 included badminton, basketball, Battleship, cricket, esports, flag football, sand volleyball, swim, soccer, table tennis, tennis, ultimate frisbee, wiffleball, rock climbing and Xtreme dodgeball.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas#cite_note-210)
